description: We are engineering students from Caucasus university, specializing in hardware and software. We are seeking new experiences and knowledge by participating in multiple contests and hackathons and resolve real life problems.
summary:
Astronauts on Mars will need to travel to remote, hard-to-reach places to do fieldwork and collect geological samples. Today, almost everything sent from the Martian surface goes through a small group of aging science orbiters. Each one passes over a given site only 2 to 4 times a day, and only while it is above the local skyline. Crater walls and ridges can hide a crew from the sky, and losing contact with a crew in an emergency is not acceptable.

Spacial Mars Mesh Systems gives a Mars crew a self-healing radio network on the surface. Lightweight relay nodes go on crater rims and ridges and form a mesh between a starting point A and a destination B. When one relay fails, traffic reroutes through its neighbours, so the crew keeps its link to base. Our open-source planner uses real NASA elevation data to do four things for a chosen site. It checks every radio link against the terrain, places the fewest relays needed to connect A and B (with a second independent route as backup), plots a safe walking route that avoids steep slopes and cliffs and stays inside radio coverage, and simulates node failures to show the network rerouting. We also designed the hardware: a solar-powered relay node and a base station built around Wi-Fi HaLow radios. Our 200 km demo is at the SpaceX Starship candidate landing site in Arcadia Planitia. It shows 63 relays and two node-disjoint routes, and the network recovers when a relay goes down.
details:
The problem:

Fieldwork on the Martian surface means sending people to rugged, poorly mapped terrain. Our team set three goals for any traverse from A to B: it must be safe, it must be efficient, and the crew must keep a communication channel the whole way.

Mars surface communications today rely on the Mars Relay Network. These orbiters are science spacecraft that relay data as a secondary job (Davis et al., NASA/JPL, 2021). The National Academies called the fleet "fragile and aging" (2018). Odyssey has been at Mars since 2001, and MAVEN's mission ended in June 2026. Each orbiter passes over a site only a few times a day, and the terrain shortens every pass. A crew at the bottom of a crater or behind a ridge can lose contact completely. Every message to Earth also takes 4 to 24 minutes each way. Good sensors and equipment are not enough if a crew in trouble cannot reach base right away.

Our solution:

SMMS is a terrain-aware mesh network on the surface. Traffic between the crew, relays and base stays on Mars, with no orbiter pass to wait for. Light crosses 100 km in 0.33 ms, and each hop adds its own processing time. Unlike a chain of access points, where one failure breaks the whole link, the mesh has several possible routes. If one node goes down, the signal goes around it through neighbouring nodes. A base station can still reach an orbiter or a satellite service when one is overhead, so the mesh supports the existing backhaul. It does not replace it.

How the planner works:

The HaLow Relay Planner is a browser application (React, TypeScript, three.js). It runs entirely on the user's computer, with no backend and no accounts.

1. Choose a site. The user places points A and B on a 3D globe of Mars. The globe shows NASA Trek Viking MDIM 2.1 colour imagery.

2. Load real terrain. The app streams elevation for a square planning area. It reads only the parts it needs from the USGS/NASA Mars HRSC + MOLA blended global DEM (200 m), using HTTP range requests. It falls back to the MGS MOLA 463 m DEM, and then to a bundled MOLA MEGDR copy, so it also works offline.

3. Check every link. For each pair of nodes, the app samples the terrain profile along the path and accounts for Mars's curvature (radius 3389.5 km). It then calculates free-space path loss plus an ITU-R P.526 knife-edge diffraction estimate and checks line of sight and first-Fresnel-zone clearance. Each link is rated good, marginal or fail, with a plain-language reason (for example, whether a ridge or the curvature itself blocks it).

4. Plan relays automatically. The app picks the high point in each grid cell as a candidate site. It then searches for the A→B path that adds the fewest relays, using the strongest weakest link to break ties. Optionally, it finds a second path that shares no relays with the first. It also connects base stations to a visible satellite by checking the terrain skyline in that direction.

5. Analyse the network. The app classifies the network as direct, chain or mesh. A mesh needs at least two node-disjoint paths, which the app checks with a max-flow calculation. It also lists single points of failure and maps radio coverage across the area.

6. Plan a safe crew route. An A* search finds a walking route from A to B through optional waypoints. It avoids slopes steeper than 15°, keeps 300 m from cliffs steeper than 25°, keeps 150 m from deep depressions and avoids no-go zones drawn by the user. Among safe routes, it prefers ones with radio coverage. Any stretch of the route without coverage is flagged.

7. Simulate failures. The user can disable any node, or pick one at random. The app reroutes in real time: the broken route turns red and the new radio route and crew path draw in green.

The app also offers a 2D survey map with hillshade, slope hatching, contours and drainage channels, and a 3D relief view with adjustable height exaggeration. It can export and import a deployment as JSON, with the model's assumptions embedded in the file.

Hardware:

We designed two circuit boards in KiCad:

Relay node (46 × 110 mm, 2 layers, 57 parts): ESP32-S3 controller, SX1262 sub-GHz radio (868/915 MHz), solar charging (BQ24074) with a Li-ion cell, INA219 power monitor, GPS and a microSD logger.

Base station (240 × 180 mm, 12 layers, 818 parts): AMD XQR Versal space-grade SoC, two Morse Micro MM6108 Wi-Fi HaLow (802.11ah) radios with Skyworks SKY66423 front ends, a Vorago VA41630 radiation-hardened supervisor and TI TPS7H radiation-hardened power regulators.

We also built SSA Space 0.1 (Surface Station Appliance), a mesh-oriented operating system for the base station. It keeps three redundant OS banks (A/B/C) that stay read-only while the system runs from initramfs, and it can connect over Iridium satellite. We have demonstrated it in a QEMU/KVM virtual machine. It is an Earth demo, not flight-qualified.

Architecture:

A physics and planning engine in pure TypeScript (propagation, graph search, planning, coverage, cost), covered by automated tests on analytic terrain.

A background worker for heavy planning and analysis, so the interface stays responsive.

Browser terrain loaders: a streaming GeoTIFF range reader and Terrarium tile decoding.

An optional native C helper on localhost that speeds up terrain download and resampling for larger areas.

Expected impact:

SMMS turns "will the crew keep contact?" into a question a mission planner can answer before an EVA. The planner shows how many relays are needed, where they go, which nodes are single points of failure, which parts of the walking route have no coverage and what happens if a relay fails. Because the relays are light and cheap, crews or rovers can place them as they go, which lowers dependence on the aging orbiter fleet. The tool is open source and every model assumption is stated, so others can check it and extend it.

Limitations:

The radio, cost and satellite values are illustrative placeholders. Satellites are a fixed snapshot, not real orbits. The planner is a heuristic over sampled candidate sites, so "no route found" means none was found among the candidates, not that none exists. Terrain detail is limited by the source DEM resolution. These limits are shown in the app and included in every export.

Data and imagery:

ESA/DLR/FU Berlin Mars Express HRSC stereo data (part of the blended Mars DEM)

Scientific and technical references:

Friis free-space path loss and first-Fresnel-zone clearance

National Academies, *Visions into Voyages for Planetary Science*, mid-term review, 2018 ("fragile and aging")

Algorithms: Dijkstra, A* search, max-flow with node splitting (node-disjoint paths), priority-flood depression filling, chamfer distance transform
